name: LLM Inference and the KV Cache
intent: Understand why serving a language model is limited by GPU memory and memory bandwidth, not by raw compute, and how the KV cache decides how many users one GPU can hold.
scenario: A chat assistant runs an 8B-class model on one 80 GB GPU. Each conversation has about 8,000 tokens of context. With one user it feels instant; as users arrive, the GPU runs out of memory long before it runs out of arithmetic, and the 53rd user has to wait.
problem: A model produces text one token at a time, and each new token needs the keys and values of every token before it. Recomputing them every step would be absurdly slow, so servers keep them in a KV cache in GPU memory. That cache grows linearly with sequence length and with the number of concurrent sequences, and it competes with the model weights for a fixed pool of expensive memory. Every decode step also has to stream the weights and the whole cache through the memory bus. Capacity (how many sequences fit) and speed (how fast each token comes out) are both set by memory, so capacity planning looks nothing like a CPU service.

howItWorks.title: Autoregressive decoding: one token per forward pass
howItWorks.text: The model predicts the next token from everything so far, appends it, and repeats until it emits a stop token. Tokens of one response cannot be computed in parallel because each depends on the previous one. A 500 token answer is 500 sequential passes through the whole network. Latency is therefore the number of output tokens times the time of one pass.

howItWorks.title: Prefill: the prompt is processed in parallel
howItWorks.text: Before the first output token, the model reads the whole prompt in one pass. All prompt tokens are independent inputs at this point, so the GPU does large matrix multiplications at high utilisation. Prefill is compute-bound (limited by arithmetic speed): its cost grows with prompt length and it sets time to first token (TTFT). Rough cost is 2 x parameters FLOPs (arithmetic operations) per prompt token, so an 8B model needs about 16 GFLOPs per token and a 8,000 token prompt takes roughly 0.5 to 1 second on one modern GPU at realistic utilisation. Attention adds a term that grows with the square of the prompt length, which this page ignores.

howItWorks.title: Decode: memory-bandwidth-bound
howItWorks.text: Each decode step handles one new token per sequence, so the arithmetic per weight is tiny. The GPU must still read every weight (16 GB for 8B parameters in 16-bit) plus every sequence's cached keys and values from high-bandwidth memory. At roughly 2 TB/s that is on the order of 8 ms per step. The time is set by bytes moved divided by bandwidth, not by FLOPs. This is what memory-bandwidth-bound means: the limit is how fast data moves out of memory. This gap between prefill and decode is why serving systems treat the two phases differently. The time between successive tokens is the inter-token latency (ITL).

howItWorks.title: The KV cache: keep keys and values, do not recompute
howItWorks.text: Attention at each layer needs a key and a value vector for every earlier token. They never change once computed, so the server stores them. Size per token = 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes per value. For 32 layers, 8 kv heads, head_dim 128 and 16-bit values that is 128 KiB per token, about 1 GB for an 8,000 token conversation. It grows linearly with tokens and linearly with the number of concurrent sequences. Without it each step would redo the work for the whole history, so cost per token would grow with the history length.

howItWorks.title: Memory sets concurrency, bandwidth sets throughput
howItWorks.text: Usable GPU memory minus the weights is the KV budget; dividing by per-sequence cache gives the maximum number of concurrent sequences. Batching several sequences into one decode step shares the weight read, so throughput rises with batch size, but each sequence's cache must still be read every step, so step time rises too. Past the point where cache reads dominate the weights, more batching buys little. Real engines allocate the cache in small blocks (paged attention) so that reserved-but-unused space does not waste capacity, and they batch continuously; see continuous-batching-and-model-serving.

howItWorks.title: Mitigations: fewer kv heads, smaller numbers, less cache
howItWorks.text: Grouped-query attention (GQA) shares each key/value head across several query heads: 8 kv heads instead of 32 cuts the cache 4x with a small quality cost, and multi-query attention (1 kv head) goes further. Quantising the cache to 8-bit halves it again and 4-bit quarters it, at some accuracy risk that must be evaluated on your tasks. Other levers: shorter contexts, sliding-window attention, evicting or compressing old tokens, sharing a common prompt prefix across requests, and offloading cold cache to CPU memory at a latency cost.

pros: The KV cache turns per-token cost from growing with the history into roughly constant compute per step
A simple formula (2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes x tokens) lets you plan GPU capacity on paper
GQA and cache quantisation multiply concurrency without new hardware
Splitting prefill from decode makes the two latency numbers (TTFT and ITL) separately tunable
cons: The cache competes with the weights for scarce, expensive GPU memory and caps concurrency
Long contexts are costly: one 128k token conversation can occupy as much cache as dozens of short ones
Decode leaves most of the GPU's arithmetic idle unless you batch, and batching raises per-user latency
Cache quantisation and aggressive eviction can quietly degrade answer quality
whenToUse: Capacity planning for any self-hosted LLM: how many concurrent users per GPU at a given context length
Choosing a model or configuration: kv heads, cache precision and maximum context length have direct cost consequences
Diagnosing latency: separate slow TTFT (prefill, prompt length) from slow ITL (decode, batch size, cache size)
whenNotToUse: You call a hosted model API: the provider owns this problem and you see it only as price per token and rate limits. Count tokens and cache hits, not gigabytes
Tiny models or short prompts where the cache is a few MB and weights dominate: tune batching, not the cache
Training: gradients and optimiser state dominate memory there; see distributed-training-and-parallelism
pitfalls: Planning capacity from weights alone: a model that fits on the GPU may leave room for only a handful of long conversations
Sizing for the average context length when a few very long requests arrive together and exhaust memory
Reporting only tokens per second per GPU: throughput can look great while each user waits a long time between tokens
Ignoring max output tokens: the cache keeps growing during generation, so a runaway answer holds memory for its whole length
Quantising the cache without re-running your evaluation set, then discovering long-context quality dropped
Treating the roofline numbers as exact: real engines add scheduling overhead, kernel inefficiency and attention cost, so measure on your hardware

roles.label: Client
roles.description: A user whose chat request carries a prompt and waits for streamed tokens.

roles.label: Inference engine
roles.description: Schedules requests, batches sequences and allocates KV cache memory.

roles.label: GPU compute
roles.description: Runs the forward pass: matrix multiplies in prefill, weight streaming in decode.

roles.label: KV cache (HBM)
roles.description: Keys and values of every token so far, held in GPU memory next to the weights.

quiz.question: A chat service runs an 8B model on one 80 GB GPU. The weights take 16 GB and the server keeps 8 GB for activations and overhead. Each conversation holds about 8,000 tokens, and its KV cache takes about 1 GB. Roughly how many conversations can run at the same time?
options: About 80, one conversation for each GB of total GPU memory
About 56, the memory left after weights and overhead
About 64, the memory left once the weights are subtracted
About 16, one conversation for each GB the weights occupy
quiz.explanation: The KV budget is total memory minus weights minus overhead, which is 56 GB, so about 56 conversations at 1 GB each. Ignoring the overhead gives 64, ignoring the weights gives 80, and 16 is only the size of the weights. With the exact 1.07 GB per conversation used elsewhere on this page it is 52, and the next user waits even though the GPU has arithmetic to spare.

quiz.question: A self-hosted model serves 256 sequences per batch and the GPU dashboard shows about 2,100 tokens per second in total, which looks excellent. Users complain that streamed text feels slow, with about 120 ms between tokens. What is the most direct change?
options: Cut the prompt length, since prompt processing sets the gap between tokens
Increase the batch size so the weight read is shared by more sequences
Add a response cache so repeated prompts skip generation entirely
Lower the maximum batch size or spread users over more GPUs
quiz.explanation: Each decode step reads the weights and every sequence's cache, so a bigger batch makes each step longer and the gap between tokens grows even as total throughput rises. Prompt length drives time to first token, not the gap between tokens, so shortening prompts does not address this symptom.

quiz.question: A team sizes GPU memory for 50 concurrent sequences at their average length of 4,000 tokens. About 1 request in 20 carries a 100,000-token document, and the cache for one of those is around 12 GB. At peak, several arrive together and the server hits out-of-memory errors. What is the best fix?
options: Admit requests by their worst-case cache need, with token caps
Add more CPU cores to the inference host so scheduling keeps up
Raise the batch size so the long requests finish sooner
Shorten the system prompt to lower the average context length
quiz.explanation: Cache memory is set by the worst cases that overlap, not by the average, so admission has to be based on reserved cache and hard caps on context and output length. A shorter average prompt barely changes the peak when a few huge requests land together.
